description: We are a passionate multidisciplinary team of 4 (developers, designers, and storytellers) taking part in NASA Space Apps Challenge 2026 in Oral (Uralsk).
summary: ReStory is an interactive 3D museum of the spacecraft humanity left behind on the Moon, Mars and beyond. Visitors fly over NASA surface maps of the Moon and Mars to the real landing sites, where each machine stands at its catalogued coordinates, and open a museum page where the machine tells its own story in the first person: why it was built, what it went through and why it fell silent. The catalog holds 28 objects, from the Apollo 11 descent stage to Ingenuity, with NASA photos credited to their authors, NASA 3D models that can be turned by hand, and "Then and now" views that pair a mission-era photo with a present-day orbital image of the same site. An AI guide answers questions using only the museum's NASA-sourced texts. ReStory runs in any browser, falls back to a text catalog on devices without 3D, and speaks English, Russian and Kazakh, so schools and museums in our region can use it too.
details:
What it does

ReStory turns abandoned spacecraft into museum exhibits that speak for themselves. The visitor sees a 3D scene with the Moon, Mars, Earth, the Sun and the other planets. Selecting an object flies the camera to its real landing site, where a NASA 3D model of the craft stands on the surface. "Learn more" opens the object's museum page: a first-person story, key facts, dates and location, a NASA photo with its author, a NASA 3D model that can be turned by hand, sister missions and links to the sources. Turning Moon and Mars globes at the sides of the page show where every object is and open any other one in a click. "Then and now" pairs an archival photo with a present-day image of the same site from the Lunar Reconnaissance Orbiter, HiRISE or the Perseverance rover. The AIstronaut guide answers visitors' questions in three languages, only from the museum's knowledge base, and says so when it does not know.

The catalog

28 objects: 11 on the Moon (from Apollo 11, Apollo 12 ALSEP, the Apollo 15 rover and Surveyor 3 to LCROSS and Lunokhod 1), 11 on Mars (from Viking 1 and Sojourner to InSight and Ingenuity), Dawn at Ceres, NEAR Shoemaker on Eros, Philae on comet 67P, MASCOT on Ryugu, Pioneer 10 and 11 and Kepler. Facts, dates and coordinates come from NSSDCA records and mission pages, and every fact links to its source.

How it works

- Server: Python, Django 5.2 and PostgreSQL with a JSON API. The whole catalog (coordinates, dates, stories in three languages, photo credits, sources) lives in one data file loaded into the database by migrations.

- Browser: plain JavaScript modules and Three.js on WebGL, no build step. NASA glTF models are Draco-compressed and decoded in the browser.

- Performance: surface maps load at 2k first and switch to 4k and 8k in the background; a 3D model loads only when the camera reaches its object and is freed when it leaves; the 3D scene pauses while a museum page is open; all libraries and assets are served locally with cache versioning.

- AI guide: a local open language model (Ollama) answers from passages retrieved from the museum texts with pgvector (retrieval-augmented generation), so it does not invent facts.

Benefits and impact

- One place where a non-expert can see where each machine is, what it did and what its site looks like today.

- Every fact links to its source; every photo and 3D model names its author.

- English, Russian and Kazakh, so schools and museums in Kazakhstan can use it on a kiosk or a phone.

- The museum grows with every mission that ends: a new object is one entry in the data file.

Creativity

The machines speak in the first person, which turns hardware into characters with a life story. The visitor moves from space to the landing site to the museum page in one continuous flight, and "Then and now" shows that this heritage is still there today.

Factors we considered

- Accuracy: real coordinates and dates, only NASA and partner agency sources, authors credited.

- Access: works on desktop and phone, respects "reduced motion", and opens a text catalog when a device cannot draw 3D instead of failing.

- Respect for heritage: Apollo 11 shows only the descent stage, which is what stayed on the Moon; models are scaled up for visibility and the page says so.

Tools

Python, Django, PostgreSQL, pgvector, JavaScript, Three.js, WebGL, glTF, Draco, HTML, CSS, Ollama, Git, GitHub.

Use of SI

ReStory was designed and mostly built by the team. AI assistants provided a starting base and helped in places with code, documentation and translations; the team extended, reviewed and tested everything. No generated images, audio or video are used: all imagery comes from NASA and partner agencies. The AIstronaut guide is itself an AI feature running a local open model.
